sourceInformation.source: The Wire (HBO, 2002-2008), created by David Simon; kept as gritty and real as the show
sourceInformation.genre: Surveillance and stealth investigation, with a case-board puzzle, a wiretap listening game and a foot chase
sourceInformation.perspective: The engine's three-quarter view (pitch 55) as the main view; the player can switch to isometric or top-down at any time
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.1 (full engine edition, one file, no dependencies); AI Hub Session Protocol v1 client 1.3.0 (session.js); plain JavaScript bundled into one HTML file by a Node build script
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's native retro-modern pixel look: 320x240 base expanded to any screen, HD Humanoid rigs, TileMap rowhouses with per-pixel painted brick, formstone, boarded vacants and graffiti, objects as data (cars, dumpster, couch, payphone, desks, reel decks), canvas lighting with street lamps, rain at night
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's procedural Humanoid rigs driven by velocity and poses, the Mover for the player (sprint, sneak, vault), scene transitions and tweens; no frame lists
sourceInformation.audio: Code-written chip-synth music (title blues, corner boom-bap, night, wire room, chase, office, ending), code-written sound effects (shutter, whistle, pager, ram, siren, cuffs), and gibberish Simlish-style voices with a pitch and timbre per speaker, blipped as the text types
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, ghost mode: each player runs their own seeded 3-minute surveillance shift, the other detectives show as ghosts with names and scores, and progress and score results go to the hub. Local 1-2 player drop-in outside the hub
sourceInformation.testing: Headless Node tests (a full five-tape playthrough with 49 checks, 52 system checks, a 16-scene smoke test); Playwright screenshots in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit; viewport-matrix on 24 phone, tablet and desktop configurations; the AI Hub harness with 1, 2 and 4 players, latency, jitter, loss and host-leave
sourceInformation.research: None beyond the engine and hub documentation; details of the show from memory
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown

testingFeedback: 28 issues, found by the headless playthrough and system tests, the browser screenshots and the viewport matrix. The AI Hub harness passed on its first run.

5 critical: a boot step that crashed the start, a runner whose stash spot was inside a wall (the corner stalled forever), a dialog carried into the next scene that froze it, the shift mode triggering story events, and a sale timer left over from the tail that meant later sessions had no sales.
The scripted headless playthrough of all five tapes. It drives the real scenes through game.advance and game.debug, and it found every soft-lock in the story chain.
The viewport matrix: 24 of 24 clean on the first run, because the engine's expand mode already fits every screen. It only caught a toast overlapping the objective box on narrow screens.
engineFeedback: The standard features are already built: the pause menu, rebinding, button glyphs per device, settings that save, fixed-step determinism, and a headless mode where the same game runs in Node for tests.

Several guesses: whether an intent object passed to Mover.update uses ground or screen directions (ground), what a face painter returns for the base colour (null), that objects as data are written facing south (my cars came out sideways at first), and that TileMap.bounds needs a view object, not a view name.
The surveillance layer: a camera viewfinder in world space that works with the mouse, a stick and the keys; the sale cycle that photos are judged against; and the lookouts' suspicion with blending.
Working with a 1.2 MB engine through its index, without seeing pixels quickly. The per-pixel wall painter's signature also takes time to learn.
The loosely checked option objects on draw calls: a typo in an option key is silently ignored.
Ship PlayStation and Xbox button symbols as font glyphs, so prompts drawn with E.font can show them without custom drawing.
promptFeedback: It is specific about the player's experience (a 10-foot UI, glyphs that follow the last device, an attract mode, the touch-only notice) and leaves the genre and design open.
'Follow the hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own' can be read as hub only, or as hub plus local multiplayer. I did both.
Fitting the show's slow, procedural texture (paperwork, waiting, minimization) into mechanics that are still fun in a short demo.
A real DualSense on a real TV at ten feet, to judge text size and glyph readability with human eyes.

aiHub.name: REWIRED
aiHub.tagline: Walk the corner. Build the board. Work the wire.
aiHub.description: An original surveillance game in the spirit of The Wire: blend in on a West Baltimore corner, photograph hand-to-hands, pin evidence to a case board and minimize calls on a wiretap. In a hub round, everyone works the same corner for one shift.
aiHub.controls: Left stick or WASD to move, L2 or right mouse to raise the camera, R2 or left click for a photo, Circle or C to crouch, Cross or E to interact
